statement.p: Let f(x,y) = 1/x + 2/y + 3 x + 4 y in the region R where x, y > 0.
Explain why f must have a global minimum at some point in R (note that R is unbounded---how does this influence your explanation?). Then find the global minimum.

static.solution:
f is continuous in the region R, but R is not closed and bounded so a special analysis is required.
Notice that f(x,y) tends to \infty as (x,y) tends farther and farther from the origin or tends toward any point on the x or y axis. This suggests that a minimum for f, if it exists, can not be too far from the origin or too close to the axes. For example, if x > 10 then f(x,y) > 3 x > 30, and if y > 10 then f(x,y) > 4 y > 40. If 0\lt x\lt 0.1 then f(x,y) > 1/x > 10, and if 0\lt y\lt 0.1 then f(x,y) > 2/y > 20.
Since f(1,1)=10, a global minimum for f if it exists must be in the smaller region R^\prime: 0.1 \le x \le 10, 0.1 \le y \le 10. The region R^\prime is closed and bounded and so have a minimum value at some point in R^\prime, and since that value is at most 10, it is also a global minimum for all of R.
Since the region R has no boundary, the minimum value must occur at a critical point of f. At a critical point we have f_x = -{1\over x^2} + 3 = 0 = f_y = -{2\over y^2} + 4 = 0. The only critical point is (\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}, \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}), at which f achieves the minimum value f(\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}},\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}) = 2\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{8}
